conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the neurology doctors. You came in with nausea, vomiting, and dizziness—can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I woke up around 7:30 last night feeling really sick. I had this wave of nausea and started vomiting. At the same time, I felt like I couldn’t stand straight—like I was floating or unsteady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Did you feel like the room was spinning, or was it more like you were off balance?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not spinning—just unsteady. I tried to get out of bed but had to sit back down. I also got a headache in the back of my head and neck. It was tight and pounding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vision changes, slurred speech, or weakness in your arms or legs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. I could talk fine, see clearly, and move my arms and legs. But I just felt too shaky to stand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve given you some anti-nausea medication and fluids. Your blood sugar is high at 296, and your INR is 1.8—slightly below your target since you’re on warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Coumadin for years because of my atrial fibrillation. Should I be worried about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring it closely. Right now, we’re more concerned about the dizziness and unsteadiness. Given your symptoms, we’re worried about a possible stroke in the back of the brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A stroke? But I didn’t have weakness or slurred speech.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Strokes in the cerebellum—back of the brain—can cause dizziness, imbalance, and nausea without the classic symptoms. We’ve ordered a CT angiogram to check for blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, the CT scan showed a possible issue in the left side of your cerebellum. To get a clearer picture, we’re going to do an MRI of your head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it definitely a stroke?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We suspect it, but the MRI will confirm. The CT showed a small area with reduced blood flow in the left cerebellum, which supplies balance and coordination.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI is back. It confirms an acute to subacute stroke in the left cerebellum. There’s no bleeding, which is good, but we need to monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ve had a stroke? But I’m talking fine and thinking clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s in a part of the brain that controls balance, not speech or movement. That’s why you’re alert and talking well. But we saw some incoordination in your left hand during the exam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did notice my left hand was a bit clumsy. What happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re admitting you to the stroke service. We’ll monitor your neurological status, manage your blood pressure, and continue your warfarin carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had two strokes before. One in the right parietal lobe, another in the temporal area. Both were related to my atrial fibrillation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history shows that. That’s why you’re on anticoagulants. We’ll continue warfarin for stroke prevention, but we have to be cautious with dosing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your INR came back at 4.2 this morning—higher than safe with a recent stroke. We’ve held your warfarin temporarily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? High INR?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It increases bleeding risk, especially with a recent stroke. We did a head CT this morning—it shows no new bleeding or swelling. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m okay? No bleed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No bleed, and no worsening of the stroke. We’ll restart warfarin at a lower dose once your INR comes down, to keep protecting you from clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted neurosurgery because your stroke caused some swelling concern. They recommend close monitoring but no surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? I thought strokes don’t need surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most don’t. But large cerebellar strokes can swell and compress the brainstem. Yours isn’t large enough for that, so we’ll manage it medically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. You stood up this morning with help and took a few steps. Your balance is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel a little wobbly, especially when I turn my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The cerebellum helps with coordination. We’ve ordered outpatient physical therapy for balance and strength training.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been resistant to therapy before. But I’ll try this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. It’ll help prevent falls and improve your confidence in walking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Your INR is back in range, and you’re walking with minimal help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my medications? Anything changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re switching you from pravastatin to atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. It’s stronger for stroke prevention. And we’re reducing your aspirin from 325 mg to 81 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why lower the aspirin? Isn’t more better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not in your case. You’re on warfarin, so high-dose aspirin increases bleeding risk without extra protection. 81 mg is safer and still effective.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And my insulin and heart meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All staying the same. Keep checking your blood sugar. We’ll also monitor your kidney function—your labs showed some acute kidney injury, likely from dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been drinking much with all the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Now that you’re eating and drinking, your kidneys should recover. Just keep hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. You’re walking independently, no new neurological issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What should I watch for after I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call 911 if you have sudden vision loss, trouble speaking, weakness on one side, facial droop, or severe imbalance. These could mean another stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my weight? My cardiologist always wants me to watch that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—weigh yourself daily. Call your cardiologist if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day. Also, keep your neurology and primary care follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doctor. I feel lucky this wasn’t worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re absolutely right. Catching this early and getting here quickly made a big difference. Keep up with your meds and therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your diabetes is still uncontrolled. HbA1c was 7.7. Work with your doctor on tighter control to reduce future stroke risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I need to do better with my diet and insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Small steps. You’ve already taken a big one by getting care when you did. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. Stay safe and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will help you with discharge instructions and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember—physical therapy is key. It’ll help your balance and confidence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll schedule it right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re on the right path.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up soon.
